text: Hey, Dick. Hey, Davis. Hey, Ian. Hi, everyone. Welcome to AI Engineer New York. I'm super excited to be here today. My name is Allie Howe. I'm a member of technical staff at Keycard. I'm here with some amazing panelists today. We have Ian, CEO of Keycard. We have Michael Davis, Global Chief Security Architect at J.P. Morgan Chase. And we have Dick Hart, the founder of Aoth and co-creator of Oath, with us on stage today. I'm super excited to talk to all of them about intent-based authorization. And to set the stage, I want to bring to light that as more companies are looking to give their agents increased levels of autonomy, they're looking to runtime authorization to help. Runtime auth is the practice of authorizing an agent per tool call, rather than having the agent hold broad standing access that it will eventually misuse. However, is this tool call or not is never a simple question. This is because many MCP tools and APIs are coarse-grained. Humans struggle to write the perfect policy, and the environment around the agent will change as it runs. Intent can help by providing extra context so that at runtime, we can make better authorization decisions about what an agent is allowed or is not allowed to do. So to continue, I would like to talk about, really dive into, why do we need intent-based auth in the first place? Models have dramatically improved. They have bigger context windows. They're able to verify work because model vision capabilities have improved, and in many contexts, people are proclaiming that AGI is here. If the models are so good, if AGI is really here today, then why are teams struggling to give their agents more autonomy? Ian, let's start with you. You're helping many financial enterprises at Keycard. What are you seeing that's getting in the way? Well, I think broadly speaking, enterprises, especially financial services firms, regulated industries, are almost always security first. It's how they build trust in their business, and maintaining the business continuity is bar first, like the first priority. Then innovation is second, third, or fourth. Dig, how is OAuth part of the problem? How is OAuth getting in the way? Why is it not the right fit for agents? Well, when people started looking at how do we authorize agents to access something, the tool that was sitting there on the shelf was OAuth. And people grabbed that tool and says, Here's a tool. This is authorization. It should be able to solve the problem. But OAuth was not designed for this kind of world. It was designed originally for like, how do I let this website talk to this website? You know, in OAuth 2, we added scopes. Before that, it was just do anything. But it required you to be pre-registered. It's expecting that there is a browser involved and a redirect. You know, OAuth has evolved over the years to support some other things. But the agentic world is completely different. We don't know ahead of time what the agent needs to do. We need to go and make that decision over time. Different instances of an agent are going to need different kinds of things.
